blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
Endoscopic bariatric and metabolic therapies treat obesity through an endoscope passed into the stomach or small bowel, without a surgical operation; one review calls them a bridge between non-surgical care and surgery.

Two act on the stomach. An intragastric balloon is one or more silicone balloons placed in the stomach empty and then filled; it takes up space in the stomach and slows its emptying, is usually left in for up to six months and then removed, and changes nothing in the stomach permanently. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty stitches the stomach wall from inside into a narrow tube.

A 2024 joint guideline of the American and European endoscopy societies, as a 2026 review reports it, places them, used as the main treatment, in people with a body mass index of 30 or more, or of 27 to 30 with an obesity-related disease, and says that one small-bowel device, the duodenal-jejunal bypass liner, should be used only within a clinical trial.

The owner of these questions is a bariatric endoscopist.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
This section has one field, and it is the one closest to your clinic. You can explain what these procedures are. You cannot judge whether a given person should have one, or which device.

Both procedures use an endoscope — a thin, flexible tube passed down the throat to see and work inside the gut. Bariatric means to do with treating obesity. Matteo and colleagues call these therapies a bridge between non-surgical care and surgery.

Take the intragastric balloon (IGB) first. It is one or more silicone balloons. The endoscopist places them in the stomach empty and then fills them. A balloon is fully reversible and leaves no permanent change in the stomach.

Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG) is a different kind of procedure. The endoscopist stitches through the full thickness of the stomach wall, from inside, and so makes a narrow tube.

The same review by Matteo and colleagues reports what a guideline says. This book can give it only in these words: a 2024 joint guideline of the American and European endoscopy societies, as a 2026 review reports it. As the review reports it, the guideline places these therapies, used as the main treatment, in people with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or more. It also places them at 27 to 30 for people with an obesity-related disease. You have not read the guideline itself, and neither has this book.

So the question of whether either procedure suits a person has an owner: a bariatric endoscopist. Here is where to find that owner.

Field Owner Where to look
Endoscopic and device therapies for obesity a bariatric endoscopist a gastroenterology department; ask which of its endoscopists has specialised training in bariatric endoscopy

The advice to ask about specialised training comes from a 2025 review by Zhai and colleagues, which says ESG “should only be performed by endoscopists with specialized training in bariatric endoscopy and obesity management”. Who in India decides whether a person is eligible is not in any source this book holds. Book 47, Metabolic and bariatric surgery: selection and co-management, teaches selection and shared care.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with what the field can answer that you cannot. Open the 2026 review by Matteo and colleagues in the Journal of Clinical Medicine, at https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm15082832. Search for ASGE–ESGE. The letters name the American and European endoscopy societies. Find the two sentences that report their guideline.

The first sentence says who the therapies are for.

according to current ASGE–ESGE guidelines, primary EBMTs are generally indicated for patients with BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2, or BMI 27–30 kg/m2 with obesity-related comorbidities

Read the signs in it. EBMTs are the review’s short name for endoscopic bariatric and metabolic therapies. The sign ≥ reads “or more”, so the review’s “BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2” is a body mass index of 30 or more, in kilograms per square metre (kg/m2 in this book). “Primary” is the guideline’s word. The same review describes these therapies also as a bridge before surgery, for people with a much higher body mass index, so read “primary” as “used as the main treatment, not as a step before surgery”.

The second sentence is about one device, the duodenal-jejunal bypass liner, which works in the duodenum and jejunum, the first parts of the small bowel. The review writes DJBL for it.

Reflecting the limited number of patients studied and short-term randomized data, the ASGE–ESGE guideline recommends that DJBL treatment should be performed only within the context of a clinical trial

Put the two in plain words. As the review reports it, the guideline sets who the therapies are for by body mass index. It keeps one device inside trials because few patients have been studied.

Now see what the review says the field weighs, and you cannot. Search for Main contraindications, the conditions that rule a balloon out.

Main contraindications to IGB placement include a history of gastrointestinal surgery, clotting or bleeding disorders, peptic ulcer disease, large hiatal hernia, structural abnormalities of the esophagus or pharynx, and pregnancy

In plain words: earlier surgery on the gut, a tendency to bleed, an ulcer in the stomach or duodenum, part of the stomach pushed up through the diaphragm, a malformed gullet or throat, and pregnancy. Then search for Severe complications.

Severe complications, although uncommon, include mucosal injury or perforation of the stomach or esophagus, gastric ulceration or bleeding, and gastrointestinal obstruction secondary to balloon migration or spontaneous rupture

In plain words: damage to the lining of the stomach or gullet, or a hole through it; an ulcer or bleeding; and a blocked gut because the balloon moved or burst. Weighing these against one person’s history is the endoscopist’s job.

Last, read the review’s own caution. Search for viewed with caution.

given the limited long-term data and modest sample sizes for many technologies, their role should be viewed with caution

This is the field’s kind of answer: who a procedure is for, who should not have it, and what can go wrong.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: You are reading a review’s report of the guideline, not the guideline. You do not have its own words, how strong it judged the evidence, or its full list of positions. Nothing here says who in India performs these procedures or decides who is eligible, and a body mass index in the stated range does not by itself make anyone suitable.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
A made-up visit. The woman of 52 who teaches at a government school comes to the OPD for her diabetes tablets. She has seen a private hospital’s hoarding for a “balloon” that takes weight off “without surgery”. The offer price ends this month. “Should I book it this week?”

The first signal is About to act. She will book on what you say. Behind it sits No test: you cannot say what result would show your answer wrong. The fifth signal turns that doubt into a duty to stop.

Start with what you can do in her visit. You can measure her weight and height and work out her body mass index. You can list her tablets and her recent sugar readings. You can tell her, in plain words, what a balloon is: placed in the stomach with an endoscope, filled there, taken out within months, and, as the review puts it, “the effects are temporary”. All of that is yours.

Two lines tempt you, and both are improvising. “The balloon is safer than surgery, so go ahead.” That compares risks you cannot check. “Those balloons do not work; just keep taking your tablets.” That claims a result you cannot show, to a woman who may then give up an option without anyone assessing her.

What you say to her: “That is outside what I can assess, and here is who can: a bariatric endoscopist. I will send one your question this week. Please wait for the reply before you book, and keep taking your diabetes tablets as before.” So write the question you would ask a bariatric endoscopist, in the five parts.

Part What you write
Decision Whether she books an intragastric balloon at the private hospital this month, and whether I refer her for an opinion first. She wants to book this week; the offer ends this month.
Context A woman of 52 with obesity and diabetes, on tablets from this centre. Her body mass index measured today, her tablets and her sugar readings for the last six months are attached. She reports no previous surgery on her stomach or gut.
Question Is an intragastric balloon a suitable option for her, and if it might be, what would you need to see before deciding, and what happens to her diabetes treatment around the procedure?
Form A recommendation: suitable, not suitable, or needs assessment, with what the assessment involves. Tell me how sure you are and on what. I cannot judge the procedure or the device.
Deadline Within two weeks. If later, I will ask her to wait for your reply before she books.

Last, the row for your contact list. Put it in now and leave the name for you to fill.

Field Owner Name and institution How you know them Last question asked Asked on Checked on
Endoscopic and device therapies a bariatric endoscopist (yours to fill) Is an intragastric balloon suitable for this patient, and what happens to her diabetes treatment around it?

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: If she only asks what a balloon is, tell her; you can. Route the question when she asks whether she should have one, or which kind. And routing does not hand her over: she remains your patient for her diabetes while she waits for the reply.

points.html: Do not tell a patient which device is better, or that a balloon “works” or “does not work”. Explain what the procedure is, and route whether it suits her to a bariatric endoscopist.

Cite the guideline only as you hold it: “a 2024 joint guideline of the American and European endoscopy societies, as a 2026 review reports it”. You have not read the guideline. Do not give its evidence grades or say how strongly it recommends anything.

A body mass index in the reported range does not make a person suitable. The review lists conditions that rule a balloon out, among them earlier surgery on the gut, bleeding disorders, peptic ulcer and pregnancy. Weighing them for one person is the endoscopist’s job.
A balloon’s effect is temporary: it is taken out, usually within six months, and leaves the stomach unchanged.
Routing ends your answer, not your care. While the endoscopist decides, she is still your patient for her diabetes.

blocks.prompt: In one line each, what are an intragastric balloon and endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty, and who owns the question of whether a patient should have one?
blocks.answer: An intragastric balloon is one or more silicone balloons placed in the stomach through an endoscope, filled there, and removed, usually within six months; it takes up space and slows emptying. Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty stitches the stomach wall from inside into a narrow tube. The owner is a bariatric endoscopist.

blocks.prompt: A made-up request. A private hospital writes to the district NCD officer offering “balloon camps” at a reduced price for people found to have obesity in the district’s screening. The officer asks you, before next month’s review meeting, whether the district should pass on the offer to the people screened. Write the question you would send to a bariatric endoscopist, in the five parts.
blocks.answer:
Part What you write
Decision Whether the district passes the offer to people found to have obesity in screening; the district NCD officer decides at next month’s review.
Context Adults screened in the district programme; their body mass index and some blood sugar results are recorded; the hospital offers intragastric balloons in camps; no individual assessment is described in the offer.
Question Is a camp the right setting to offer intragastric balloons to people found in screening, and what assessment and follow-up should each person have before and after?
Form A recommendation: pass it on, pass it on with conditions (which), or do not. Tell me how sure you are and on what. I cannot judge the procedure.
Deadline Two weeks before the review, so the officer can reply to the hospital. If later, the offer is not passed on until the next review.

Whether the district may pass on a private offer at all is a question for the district’s administrative officer, not the endoscopist.

blocks.prompt: A made-up line from a health column: “The new stitching procedure done through the mouth is as good as surgery and safer, so everyone with obesity and diabetes should ask for it.” Name the first signal that should fire in the writer, and rewrite the line.
blocks.answer:
About to act fires first: readers will ask for a procedure on the strength of the line. The writer is also past the edge, with nothing they could check. “As good as surgery and safer” and “everyone” are claims about outcomes and eligibility.

A rewrite: “Endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty narrows the stomach by stitching it from inside. Whether it suits a particular person is for a bariatric endoscopist to judge. If you have obesity and diabetes and want to know your options, ask your doctor for a referral.”
